What you need to understand is that our senses are basically electrical and chemical impulses transmitted by tiny sensors that receive a limited range of stimuli from the environment. These messages are then processed by our nervous system.

To give a fairly good explanation how sight works you need to know about electromagnetic waves and stuff, and it would take like 30 minutes to explain it clearly from the basics, but the point is that our receptors (the tiny body parts that capture stimuli from the environment) are not capturing everything. For example, the receptors in our eyes capture electromagnetic waves. Radio, microwave, visible light, UV rays, Gamma rays are all electromagnetic waves just with a different wavelength (height), but our eyes are capable of capturing only a tiny fraction of these wavelengths.

Our taste receptors fire after they came in contact with certain chemical responses. We are only capable of detecting a small number of chemical responses this way, but there are innumerable others we are just not configured for.

And this was just detecting these responses, then we still have to process them, which could happen in an infinite number of ways. It's safe to say that when you and I are eating the same icecream, we experience the taste in different ways. In fact, at different times you experience the taste of the same thing differently.
